newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: DUTCH THE FIRST MARKET TO BE FLOODED BY SMARTCARDS.
newsitem.headline: DUTCH THE FIRST MARKET TO BE FLOODED BY SMARTCARDS.

text.p: Dozens of smartcard trials are carried out across the globe and industry pundits forecast billions of these computer cards will be in circulation at the beginning of the next millenium, but Dutch banks are the first in the world to introduce them on a nationwide scale this year.

This month, banks in the Netherlands will start issuing smartcards to their clients so that by October 1997 all 15 million people in the Netherlands will be able to live their lives without having to carry cash.
The Dutch smartcards are not just reloadable cash cards, but can also be used for on-line bank transfers, retail loyalty schemes such as airmiles, teleshopping and ticket reservation.

A Dutch consumer can store small amounts of cash on a card which can be used for purchases such as icecream or bus fare. The money will be transferred from the card to the retailer's without costly on-line telecom links via the bank.
More expensive articles will ideally be paid on-line, validated by the client's secret four digit individual code.
Smart cards can be loaded at "cash dispensers", but by the end of 1996 also at home via smartphones or cheap "home-loaders" connected to an ordinary telephone.
"The Netherlands is forerunner. We're the first country to introduce smartcards on a national scale," said a spokesman for the Dutch "chipknip" (chip purse) consortium.

Typically, there will be two types of Dutch smartcards, issued by two groups of banks, Rabobank and ABN AMRO on one side with their "Chipknip" and Postbank and PTT Telecom on the other with their "Chipper".
"Our card has slightly more computer memory which will make payment transactions more secure," the Chipknip spokesman said.
The Chipper consortium on the other hand claims its card has a multifunctional character.

"It's a services card. You can also use it to book cinema tickets and then go the theatre where your card is swiped at the entrance for identifaction. You don't need a physical paper ticket anymore," a Chipper spokesman said.
The Chipknip consortium says such applications will also possible with their card in the near future.
"We're still expanding the functions," he said.

The computer chips on the current generation of smartcards can hold as much of four densely typed A4 pages of information but the industry keeps expanding capacity in the fight for this potential multibillion dollar market.
The more information can be stored on one card, the fewer smartcards consumers will have to carry around.
Trials in the U.S., such as the one in Atlanta at summer olympic games by Visa , focus on payment transactions.

But the Spanish and French governments will launch smartcards on a massive scale next year to make health care and social security safer and more efficient. Citizens will carry their medical or social records on a card.
Public transport is another greenfield for smartcards as it reduces ticket sales time and fare-dodging.

Contactless fare collection is currently pioneered in South Korea's Seoul, using systems developed by Mikron Indentification, an Austrian company which was bought by Philips Electronics in 1995 and which also runs pilots in Sydney.
Smartcards are also used to personalise GSM telephones, computers and pay-television.

Although the first smartcard was developed as early as in 1977 by Motorola and Bull in 1977 for a bank in France, the home of the smartcard, they are only now catching on, but without one standard leading the industry.
The choice for an encryption method to ensure safety is still being debated and so is that for contactless reading.

The battle over the smartcard technology and licence fees is fought between a few companies, giants as Motorola, Bull, Philips, Visa and Mastercard but also LSI , Thomson and specialised France's Gemplus and Britain's Mondex.

But Dutch banks and retailers, who will have to carry most of the costs of rolling out the infrastructure, do not wait for a single standard, despite higher costs of adapting to different systems in a later stage. The advantages are far too clear.
Dutch unions have warned that thousands of banking jobs will be lost due to the introduction of smartcards. The banks themselves had already realised this. -- Amsterdam Newsroom +31 20 504 5000
